1:
The relation of this psalm to the song in the Chronicles account of the ark divides the entry before a word of it is expounded. Adam Clarke notes that it carries no title in the Hebrew or Chaldee, while the Syriac calls it a prophecy of the advent of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles, and the Greek and Latin versions head it as a song of David from when the house was built after the captivity; he concludes that the Chronicles ode has thirty verses and this is only a section of it, lifted out to serve at the dedication of the second temple. John Calvin agrees and adds a detail: the opening verse is not in the original poem at all, but appears to have been added for the new occasion. Keil and Delitzsch reverse the direction. The chronicler took this psalm up almost entire, and the coarse seams at either end of his quotation show that he was stringing familiar reminiscences together as a mosaic to express the mood of that day; the Greek title still correctly interprets the psalm as post-exilic, and its key-note, that the religion of the Lord is destined for mankind at large, is deutero-Isaianic. Charles Ellicott calls it a kind of national and religious lyric cry after the Restoration. John Wesley waves the question aside: the occasion is not the removal of the ark but the coming of the Messiah.

What makes the song new is disputed as well. Matthew Henry takes it as the product of new affections clothed with new expressions, a song for favours that are new every morning, a New Testament song for the new covenant — and one that shall never wax old, though we call nothing more despicable than an old song. Adam Clarke restricts the word to quality: new here means of peculiar excellence, as the term is repeatedly used in Scripture. John Calvin denies that it is new absolutely; it is called new from having been adapted to a new purpose, and the word must point to some unusual and extraordinary display of the divine goodness, the erecting of God’s kingdom in a manner altogether unlooked for. John Gill refers it to the new benefit of redemption lately obtained by the Messiah. Augustine of Hippo makes the newness moral: the lust of the flesh sings the old song and the love of God the new, and since the psalm is titled of a house building after the captivity, the very act of singing is the building — a house raised in no one spot and no particular region.

The threefold summons draws its own comment. John Gill reports that the third naming of the divine name has led some to think of the three Persons, the Father contriving salvation, the Son effecting it and the Spirit applying it, and Matthew Henry makes the same division without arguing for it. On declaring the glory among the heathen Adam Clarke distinguishes the audiences: to the Gentiles, who do not know the true God, declare his splendour and excellence, since his being and attributes are the foundation of all religion; to the Jews declare his wonders, the miracles wrought in Judea. Matthew Henry hears the apostles’ commission copied from the verse. C.H. Spurgeon hears instead a silence falling: the hymns of Jupiter and Neptune, of Vishnoo and Siva, are hushed for ever, the Bacchanalian shouts stilled, the names of Baalim no more on men’s lips and the wanton music of Ashtaroth ceased, so that a Jew may invite the Gentiles to adore and join with them.
4:
The gods of the fourth verse are contested. Adam Clarke doubts that the plural name of God is ever, by fair construction, applied to false gods or idols, and would divide the clauses so that the great and greatly praised one stands alone and the Deity is to be feared above all; the contracted form used in the next verse, he thinks, carries the meaning of idols. Charles Ellicott reads the play on words the other way: the term for idols is literally nothings, with a play on the ordinary word for God, and this plainly shows that the gods of the previous verse are the heathen deities and not angels. He notes that the Greek sometimes renders the word idols and sometimes vanities but here demons, while Symmachus has nonexistences. John Gill takes them as nothings and nonentities, many of which never had any being except in the fancies of men. Matthew Henry allows princes, who were often deified after their deaths and adored as petty gods while they lived, but prefers the idols: he is great and they are little, he is all and they are nothing. John Wesley settles it in a line, that these are the gods of the nations, as the next verse expounds it.

On the honour and majesty before him Adam Clarke asks whether the reference is to the cloud of glory that preceded the ark through the wilderness, since the words used here and in the next verse are those by which the ark is described elsewhere. Charles Ellicott takes the whole universe to display that majesty but chiefly the sanctuary in Israel, where the costly splendour of the building and its rites typify it; he quotes a version rendering the line as pureness and stately glory fitting the shrine, and observes that the chronicler, adopting the psalm for the bringing up of the ark, substituted strength and gladness in his place — possibly because the temple was not yet built. John Gill fills the scene with rays of glory and attending angels, and rejects as less noble the reading of Kimchi, who makes them the stars. Matthew Henry divides the two worlds: splendour and majesty above, where the angels cover their faces, strength and beauty in the sanctuary below.

The threefold call to give is heard by Keil and Delitzsch as an echo of an earlier psalm, whose whole strophe this repeats, with the nations coming in bearing the gifts they are told to bring. Charles Ellicott identifies the offering as the sacrifice of fine flour, and Adam Clarke reads the summons narrowly, as addressed to the families and tribes of Israel in their divisions, with the courts probably those of the second temple. The last clause divides them again. Adam Clarke takes the beauty of holiness for holy ornaments, the vestments the high priest wore in his ministrations, given him for glory and beauty, so that the call is to put on the sacerdotal garments, bring the offering and make intercession for the people. Charles Ellicott renders it bow before the Lord in holy attire, noting that the Greek and Latin support the alternative, and Keil and Delitzsch defend the holy attire by the dependence on that earlier psalm, comparing the wedding garment of the parable. John Wesley takes it of the gifts and graces necessary in worship, and John Gill of the whole eastern ceremonial of approaching a king with presents and prostration. Matthew Henry hears in it the outer court of the Gentiles laid in common with the court of Israel.
10:
The tenth verse sets the preachers their message. John Gill hears a direction to the converted Jews and the first preachers of the Gospel, sent into all the world that a people might be taken from among the nations. Matthew Henry calls it an illustrious prophecy of the setting up of Christ’s kingdom upon the ruins of the devil’s, and notes that Peter was the first to say it among the heathen. Charles Ellicott reads the clause as the watchword of the Restoration — that the Lord has become King — an evangel not for Jerusalem only but for the world at large, to which is added, in a different arrangement from the chronicler’s, the statement of the stability of the world, emblem of the stability and justice of the divine government. Adam Clarke takes the established world for the habitable globe, the container put for the contained, and reports that many understand the Church; John Wesley hears the promise of an established and lasting peace among the nations, and Matthew Henry divides it three ways, the natural world upheld by the Redeemer, the world of mankind preserved till the election of grace is called in, and the church that cannot be shaken.

An ancient addition to the verse divides the two who mention it. Adam Clarke reports that Justin Martyr quotes the clause as saying the Lord ruleth from the wood, meaning the cross, and accuses the Jews of having blotted the word out because of the evidence it gave for Christianity; the reading was quoted by Tertullian, Lactantius, Arnobius, Cassiodorus, Pope Leo, Gregory of Tours and others, still stands in the ancient Roman Psalter, and appears as a marginal gloss in the manuscript Psalter before him. Yet, he adds, no such words exist in any copy of the Hebrew now extant, in any manuscript yet collated, or in any of the ancient versions; and neither Eusebius nor Jerome, both of whom wrote on the Psalms, so much as refers to it. Matthew Henry gives the same reading a shorter verdict: a gloss which some of the ancients added and which by degrees crept into the text.

Whether the rejoicing creation is figure or allegory divides the close. John Gill allegorizes throughout: the heavens are the angels, or men born from above, or the apostles and ministers full of heavenly gifts; the field is not the field of the world but of the church, a wilderness become fruitful. Adam Clarke prints the old Psalter’s version and its paraphrase, in which the heavens are holy men, the earth meek men who receive learning, the fields mild and soft men, and the trees of the wood sinful men once without fruit and since taken into God’s temple — a reading he says echoes the opinion of most of the Latin fathers, and one he does not adopt: the psalmist, in the true spirit of poetry, gives life and intelligence to universal nature, producing them all as exulting in the reign of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch ground the figure in Isaiah, who makes the trees of the wood exult and clap their hands, and again collate the chronicler, who flattens the poetic word for field into the prosaic one and drops the all before the trees. Charles Ellicott reaches for Milton, whose winds are bidden breathe soft or loud and his pines wave their tops in sign of worship. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense, the presence and approach of their Lord and Maker; and John Gill notes that the clause about being before the Lord is to be joined to every one of the two preceding verses.
